newsitem.title: HONG KONG: PRESS DIGEST - HK Newspaper Headlines - Dec 4.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - HK Newspaper Headlines - Dec 4.

text.p: These are some of the leading stories in the Hong Kong press on Wednesday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

-- SING TAO -- Britain has said 50,000 Hong Kong families who had acquired full British passports under the British Nationality Selection Scheme would not be entitled to formal consular protection in China and Hong Kong after 1997.
-- EXPRESS NEWS -- The government has no intention to suppress property prices for now but will increase land supply.
-- MING PAO -- About one third of insurance companies in Hong Kong do not have enough reserves to pay off claims.
-- Bar girls in China's Sichuan province are buying fake university certificates because clients prefer to be entertained by "educated" girls. With a forged certificate they get paid 50 per cent more

-- TIN TIN DAILY -- The number of mainland prostitutes in the territory grew by 7,000 per cent over the past three years. In Mongkok district alone, police have detained more than 1,000 mainland prostitutes so far this year.
-- TA KUNG PAO -- The government of Guangdong province has decided to crack down on fake products, and stressed that imposing fines could not replace imprisonment.

-- ECONOMIC JOURNAL -- China Resources Enterprise announced it would use $3.5 billion to buy a 10 per cent stake in Hong Kong International Terminals from its parent company China Resources (Holdings) Co.
-- ECONOMIC TIMES -- China had approved three foreign banks to operate renminbi business starting from this month. Next year more banks will be allowed to begin yuan business.
-- SOUTH CHINA MORNING POST -- A confidential draft of proposed rules showed the government intended 30 per cent of Mandatory Provident Funds to be denominated in Hong Kong assets.
-- A leading credit analyst said Hong Kong and China deserved to have their debt ratings raised following recent positive political and economic developments.
-- HONGKONG STANDARD -- China was seeking to lure foreign investors to its mining industry through revamped legislation and a strong demand for minerals.
